description: Margin, padding, border — and the box-sizing trick that keeps layouts sane.

screens.body:
Every HTML element is a rectangular box made of four layers. From the inside out: content, padding, border, margin.

The content is your text or image. Around it sit padding, then border, then margin — like rings around a target.

Once you can picture these four layers, half of all CSS layout confusion disappears.

check.question: Name the four box layers from inside out.

screens.heading: Every element is a box
screens.keyPoint: content → padding → border → margin, inside out.

screens.body:
Padding is breathing room INSIDE the box — the space between the content and the border.

The element's background color stretches through the padding, so padding makes a box look bigger and airier.

Use it when text feels cramped against the edges: padding: 16px gives everything room to breathe.

options: Between the content and the border
Between the border and the margin
check.question: Where does padding sit?

screens.heading: Padding: breathing room inside
screens.keyPoint: Padding = space inside, background shows through.

screens.body:
The border is the box's visible edge. The shorthand sets three things at once: border: 2px solid black; — width, style, color.

The style part (solid, dashed, dotted) is required — without it, no border appears, even with a width and color set.

Borders draw the eye and separate sections. border-radius: 12px rounds the corners for that modern card look.

check.question: Which border part is required for it to show?

screens.heading: Border: the visible edge

screens.body:
Margin is space OUTSIDE the box — it pushes neighboring elements away.

Unlike padding, margin is always transparent: the page background shows through. Margins create the gaps between cards, sections, and paragraphs.

The classic centering trick: margin: 0 auto; on a fixed-width block centers it horizontally in its parent.

options: It adds color around the box
check.question: What does margin do?

screens.heading: Margin: space outside

screens.body:
Here's the gotcha that breaks layouts: by default, width sets only the CONTENT width. Padding and border get added on top.

width: 200px with padding: 20px and border: 5px actually renders 200 + 40 + 10 = 250px wide.

So two "50% width" columns with padding overflow their row. This surprise has bitten every CSS developer alive.

check.question: width: 200px, padding: 20px each side, border: 5px each side. Total width?

screens.heading: Widths add up (the gotcha)
screens.keyPoint: Default width = content only; padding and border add on.

screens.body:
box-sizing: border-box; fixes the gotcha: width now means the FULL box including padding and border.

Set width: 200px with padding and border, and the whole thing stays 200px — the content area just shrinks to fit.

Most developers apply it to everything with * { box-sizing: border-box; } at the top of their stylesheet. Do this and your layouts will behave.
screens.heading: box-sizing: border-box fixes it
screens.keyPoint: border-box: width = the whole box. Use it everywhere.

screens.body:
One more quirk: vertical margins between stacked blocks collapse — they don't add up.

A box with margin-bottom: 20px above a box with margin-top: 30px leaves a 30px gap, not 50px. The bigger margin wins.

It's strange, but harmless once you know: if a gap looks smaller than your margins say, collapse is probably why.
screens.heading: Margin collapse (the weird one)
screens.keyPoint: Stacked vertical margins collapse to the larger one.
